databases.name: COCONUT (COlleCtion of Open NatUral producTs)
databases.scope: Broadest open aggregated NP collection: elucidated and predicted NPs harvested from ~60 source collections, all kingdoms
databases.compound_count: 1,122,178 molecules — read live from the production API on 2026-08-17 (POST /api/search returns total=1122178 for an empty query). Static Zenodo dump 'COCONUT 2.0 - Complete database' is frozen at 2024-10-04; the live DB has grown well past it. API self-reports version 2.0.0.
databases.licence: Conflicting and must be resolved before redistribution. Site /about states: infrastructure code MIT, 'Complete curated dataset is available for download under CC0 License'. The Zenodo dumps (10.5281/zenodo.13897048 and the two earlier versions) are tagged cc-by-4.0. CC0 vs CC BY 4.0 is a real difference for downstream attribution obligations.
databases.api_or_download_url: https://coconut.naturalproducts.net/api/search (POST, unauthenticated, works); OpenAPI spec at https://coconut.naturalproducts.net/vendor/rest/openapi.json; bulk at https://zenodo.org/records/13897048 (coconut_complete-10-2024.csv.zip 207 MB, .sdf.zip 691 MB, full SQL dump 1.82 GB)
databases.suitability: Best single anchor for a laptop pipeline, but mind two traps I hit live. (1) Only POST /api/search is open; /api/molecules and /api/molecules/search both return {"message":"Unauthenticated."}, so REST-only ingestion needs an API key. (2) Deep pagination is capped — pages 20000 and 40000 returned empty while page 5000 worked, so you cannot walk 1.1M records through the search API. Take the Zenodo SDF/CSV for bulk and use the API only for deltas and lookups. Query param is 'query', not 'q' — passing 'q' silently returns the whole table, which is an easy way to fabricate a wrong count.

databases.name: LOTUS (naturalproducts.net / Wikidata structure-organism pairs)
databases.scope: Referenced structure-organism pairs; the reference-backed provenance layer for NP occurrence, hosted in Wikidata
databases.compound_count: 674,454 (structure, organism, reference) triples; 227,319 unique structures by InChIKey; 37,468 unique organisms; 91,382 unique reference DOIs — counted by downloading and parsing the 2026-04-13 frozen dataset. Cross-validated against live Wikidata via SPARQL the same day: 544,778 chemical-taxon pairs, 227,361 distinct chemicals carrying an InChIKey, 37,550 distinct taxa. The two agree to within 0.1% on structures and organisms.
databases.licence: Underlying Wikidata statements are CC0. The Zenodo frozen exports (10.5281/zenodo.19360665, concept 10.5281/zenodo.5794106) are tagged CC BY 4.0. Cleanest redistribution position of any resource here.
databases.api_or_download_url: SPARQL at https://query.wikidata.org/sparql (times out on unindexed aggregates — I had to use the QLever mirror at https://qlever.dev/api/wikidata, Wikidata dump of 2026-08-10, updated live); frozen bulk at https://zenodo.org/records/19360665 (260413_frozen.csv.gz 20.6 MB core triplets, 260413_frozen_metadata.csv.gz 90.3 MB with structural descriptors)
databases.suitability: The provenance backbone — every row carries a literature DOI, which none of the aggregators except NPAtlas and CyanoMetDB can match. Use the Zenodo frozen CSV, not live SPARQL: query.wikidata.org returned 'upstream request timeout' and then 502 on plain COUNT aggregates over P703. Critical modelling trap: P703 ('found in taxon') is also used on gene and protein items, so an unfiltered COUNT gives 2,574,092 subjects. You must constrain to chemicals (I filtered on P235 InChIKey) or your NP count is off by an order of magnitude. Stereo: 172,871 of 227,357 structures (76%) carry an isomeric SMILES (P2017).

databases.name: NPASS (Natural Product Activity and Species Source)
databases.scope: NPs with species source AND experimentally measured quantitative bioactivity; the main open source of measured activity attached to NP provenance
databases.compound_count: v3.0, released 2025-06-15: 204,023 unique natural products, 48,940 source organisms, 1,048,756 activity records against 8,764 targets (stated on the About page). I independently downloaded the structure file: NPASS3.0_naturalproducts_structure.txt contains 192,587 structures, so ~11,400 catalogued NPs ship without a structure.
databases.licence: No licence statement anywhere on the site — I searched the home, about and download pages and found only a copyright footer. Default is all-rights-reserved. Usable internally; NOT safely redistributable without written permission.
databases.api_or_download_url: https://bidd.group/NPASS/downloadnpass.html — plain tab-delimited files, e.g. https://bidd.group/NPASS/downloadFiles/NPASS3.0_naturalproducts_structure.txt (61 MB), NPASS3.0_activities.txt, NPASS3.0_naturalproducts_species_pair.txt, NPASS3.0_species_info.txt, NPASS3.0_target.txt, NPASS3.0_toxicity.txt
databases.suitability: Highest-value bioactivity source in this set and trivial to ingest — flat TSV with np_id / InChI / InChIKey / SMILES, 73.2% of the 192,587 structures carry tetrahedral stereo (@ in SMILES). No API at all, so schedule a periodic full re-pull. Be aware the activity data is substantially integrated from ChEMBL v35, so NPASS activities and a ChEMBL ingest will overlap heavily — dedupe on assay/reference or you will double-count. Licence silence is the blocker for any redistribution.

databases.name: CMAUP (Collective Molecular Activities of Useful Plants)
databases.scope: Plant-centric: useful/medicinal plants, their chemical ingredients, human protein targets, GO/KEGG/disease associations
databases.compound_count: v2.0 (NAR 2024 update): 60,222 chemical ingredients — verified exactly by downloading CMAUPv2.0_download_Ingredients_All.txt and counting 60,222 data rows. Also verified: 7,864 plants in the Plants file (site claims 7,865), 28,871 ingredient-target activity records with values, units and references. Site states 758 targets, 1,399 diseases, 238 KEGG pathways, 3,013 GO terms.
databases.licence: No licence statement; download page carries only '© 2018 Copyright'. Treat as all-rights-reserved.
databases.suitability: Clean, small, well-normalised relational dump — 13 tab-delimited files with a readme, ingests in minutes. 69.6% of the 60,222 ingredients carry tetrahedral stereo. Organism resolution is plant-level with NCBI Taxonomy IDs at species/genus/family, which is better structured than most TCM resources. Note the activity table is only 28,871 rows — an order of magnitude smaller than NPASS, so use CMAUP for plant-target-pathway association and NPASS for activity depth. Same BIDD group as NPASS, same licence silence.

databases.name: SuperNatural III (SuperNatural 3.0)
databases.scope: Natural products and NP-based derivatives with MoA, pathway, target and disease-indication modules
databases.compound_count: UNVERIFIABLE — resource is dead. Published figures (NAR 2023, 51(D1):D654, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkac1008, verified via Crossref) were 449,058 unique natural compounds and 790,096 structures including isomers. I could not confirm these against any live instance.
databases.licence: Paper describes it as freely available without login or registration; no machine-readable licence recoverable because the host is gone.
databases.api_or_download_url: http://bioinf-applied.charite.de/supernatural_3 — DEAD. The hostname returns NXDOMAIN from both Google (8.8.8.8) and Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) DNS, so this is authoritative host removal, not a local resolver or transient outage. Parent domain charite.de resolves fine (141.42.206.113); sibling host bioinformatics.charite.de resolves; bioinf-applied, supernatural, bioinf and structure subdomains all NXDOMAIN. The bio.tools registry entry (https://bio.tools/api/tool/supernatural_3.0/) still lists the same dead homepage and records no licence and no mirror.
databases.suitability: DO NOT PLAN AROUND THIS. Despite a 2023 NAR database-issue paper and ~449k claimed unique NPs, the sole published access point no longer exists in DNS and I found no mirror. Any pipeline or proposal citing SuperNatural III as a live dependency is already broken. If you need its content, the only route is contacting the Charité group directly or recovering an archived CSV — neither is automatable.

databases.name: NPAtlas (The Natural Products Atlas)
databases.scope: Microbially-sourced NPs only — bacteria and fungi, each entry tied to its isolation publication
databases.compound_count: 36,454 compounds in DB version 2024_09 (website version 3.0.2) — verified by downloading the full 33.7 MB TSV and counting rows. Composition: 22,995 fungal, 13,459 bacterial. PubChem independently lists 'The Natural Products Atlas' as a source with 37,365 compounds.
databases.licence: CC BY-NC 4.0 (stated on the download page and in the site footer). The NonCommercial clause is a hard blocker for any commercial product or for redistribution inside a permissively-licensed aggregate.
databases.api_or_download_url: https://www.npatlas.org/download — https://www.npatlas.org/static/downloads/NPAtlas_download.tsv (33.7 MB), also .json, .sdf, .xlsx, and network graphMLs. Note /api/v1 and /api/v1/compounds return HTTP 200 but empty bodies, so there is no usable REST API despite the paths existing.
databases.suitability: The highest-quality, most reliably curated set here and the easiest single ingest — 34 well-named columns, one file. Provenance is perfect: 100% of 36,454 rows carry genus and 100% carry an original-reference DOI, plus PMIDs, MIBiG, GNPS and NPMRD cross-refs. Stereo is strong: 73.7% tetrahedral (@), 27.8% E/Z. Two constraints: it is microbial-only so it will not cover plant NPs at all, and CC BY-NC means it cannot go into a redistributable commercial library. Ingest it, keep it in a licence-partitioned table.

databases.name: CyanoMetDB
databases.scope: Secondary metabolites of cyanobacteria, manually curated from primary literature
databases.compound_count: 3,084 entries in Version 03 (release NORMAN-SLE-S75.0.3.0, dated 2024-09-28) — verified by downloading CyanoMetDB_V03_2024.csv and counting rows.
databases.licence: CC BY 4.0 (Zenodo record metadata). Cleanly redistributable with attribution.
databases.api_or_download_url: https://zenodo.org/records/13854577 (version DOI 10.5281/zenodo.13854577; concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.4551528 always resolves to latest). Files: CyanoMetDB_V03_2024.csv (3.7 MB), .xlsx, a MetFrag-ready CSV, and an InChIKey list. Also reachable as NORMAN Suspect List Exchange entry S75 (PubChem classification hierarchy hid=101). Project page https://www.eawag.ch/en/department/uchem/projects/cyanometdb/ is live. Note https://cyanometdb.github.io/ is a 404 — do not use it.
databases.suitability: Small, pristine, and the best licence-to-quality ratio in the whole survey. 40 columns; 75.8% have an isomeric SMILES and 73.9% carry tetrahedral stereo; 100% carry a reference DOI; 85.1% carry an NPAtlas ID so it joins cleanly to NPAtlas. Organism caveat worth encoding: the Genus column is populated for 100% of rows but 448 of them are the literal string 'n.a.', so true genus coverage is 2,636/3,084 (85.5%) — a naive non-null check will overstate provenance. Versioned Zenodo DOIs make this fully reproducible.

databases.name: ChEMBL natural-product subset
databases.scope: NP-flagged subset of ChEMBL's bioactivity corpus (natural_product flag on molecule_dictionary)
databases.compound_count: 98,989 molecules with natural_product=1, out of 2,921,148 distinct compounds — read live from the ChEMBL REST API. Release is ChEMBL_37, release date 2026-05-01, with 24,527,044 activities, 1,970,438 assays, 18,552 targets, 101,100 documents (confirmed against both /status.json and chembl_37_release_notes.txt).
databases.licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 Unported — I read the actual LICENSE file on the EBI FTP root. ShareAlike is the operative risk: it is copyleft, so mixing ChEMBL into a merged library can force the whole derived dataset to be licensed alike. Keep it in a separate, clearly attributed partition.
databases.api_or_download_url: REST: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/api/data/molecule.json?natural_product=1 (paginated, total_count in page_meta). Bulk: https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/chembl/ChEMBLdb/latest/ — chembl_37_chemreps.txt.gz, chembl_37.sdf.gz, chembl_37_postgresql.tar.gz, plus LICENSE and release notes.
databases.suitability: Unbeatable for measured bioactivity, but the NP flag is the weak link and you should not treat it as a clean NP set. Sampling the first 100 NP-flagged molecules, only 28 carried any stereocentre and the very first hit was a synthetic quinazoline (COc1cc2nc(N3CCN(C(=O)c4ccco4)CC3)nc(N)c2cc1OC) — the flag means 'natural-product-derived', which sweeps in heavily elaborated synthetics. Use it as a bioactivity join target keyed on InChIKey against COCONUT/LOTUS/NPAtlas rather than as an NP definition. There is also no per-compound source organism, so ChEMBL cannot supply provenance. Both REST and FTP are robust and scriptable.

databases.name: PubChem classification-based NP retrieval
databases.scope: Retrieval of NP subsets out of PubChem by Compound-TOC classification node, i.e. by which NP database annotated the compound
databases.compound_count: Verified live from the PubChem Compound TOC hierarchy (hid=72): LOTUS heading 224,662 compounds; NPASS heading 82,207; 'The Natural Products Atlas' 37,365; 'The Natural Products Atlas Classification' 36,256; 'KEGG: Natural Toxins' 281. PubChem as a whole holds 124,589,106 compounds and 348,976,205 substances (Entrez esearch, 2026-08-17).
databases.licence: PubChem's own aggregation carries no copyright restriction (US Government work); individual depositor records carry their own terms, and the classification nodes above inherit the upstream database's licence (so NPAtlas-derived CIDs remain CC BY-NC).
databases.api_or_download_url: Classification tree: https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/classification/cgi/classifications.fcgi?format=json&hid=72 (~614 KB; counts live in Information.Counts as [{"Type":"Compound","Count":N}]). Relevant HNIDs: LOTUS 4875769, NPASS 5592124, NP Atlas 4308215, NPAtlas Classification 4326270. Source table: https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/rest/pug/sourcetable/substance/JSON. Entrez: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pccompound
databases.suitability: Best used as a normalisation and cross-walk layer, not a primary NP source — it gives you standardised CIDs, InChIKeys and computed properties for NPs that other databases already identified. Several documented routes are broken and cost real time, so note them: classifications.fcgi?hid=list returns HTTP 400 'Caught ncbi::CException'; the hnid parameter is silently ignored and always returns the whole tree, so you must walk the JSON and match on Information.HNID; PUG-View annotations/heading returns 404 for all three NP heading strings; and Entrez [SRC]/[SourceName] queries for NPASS, LOTUS and COCONUT all return 0. What does work is parsing the hid=72 tree for Counts. PubChem lists no COCONUT, LOTUS or NPASS depositor in the substance source table — only NPAtlas (36,399 substances) appears as a depositor.

databases.name: ZINC-22
databases.scope: Make-on-demand and purchasable synthetic screening space, with a dedicated natural-product tranche (zinc-22np)
databases.compound_count: UNVERIFIED for the NP tranche. The zinc-22np directory is real and active (40 heavy-atom tranches H10 through H49, last modified 2025-11-24 to 2025-12-12), but it is sharded into thousands of subdirectories of gzipped SMILES; counting it would require walking the full tree, which I did not do, so I will not put a number on it. The overall ZINC-22 tree is actively maintained (generation zinc-22g last modified 2026-04-13). PubChem lists the ZINC depositor at 13,814,174 substances, which reflects ZINC-20-era deposits, not ZINC-22 scale.
databases.licence: No licence statement found on the file server or index pages. Additionally some tranches are deliberately password-protected (the index states this is to preserve composition-of-matter patentability), so parts of the corpus are explicitly not open.
databases.api_or_download_url: https://files.docking.org/zinc22/ (directory index); NP tranche at https://files.docking.org/zinc22/special/zinc-22np/ — files are per-tranche .np.smi.gz, e.g. .../zinc-22np/H10/H10M000/H10M000-N.np.smi.gz. zinc22.docking.org redirects to the CartBlanche SPA at https://cartblanche22.docking.org/, which is JavaScript-only and returns no server-rendered content.
databases.suitability: Include only if you need docking-ready synthetic analogues alongside real NPs — it is not a natural-product provenance resource. Format is minimal: two columns, SMILES and ZINC ID (e.g. 'CNC(=O)[C@H]1CCC(=O)O1  ZINCa50000001JoU'), with stereo present but no organism, no reference, no bioactivity. Practical warnings for a laptop pipeline: the tranche tree is very wide so plan a crawler with backoff rather than a recursive wget; the absence of any licence plus deliberately password-gated sections makes redistribution untenable; and the CartBlanche front end cannot be scraped without a headless browser.

databases.name: Dictionary of Natural Products (DNP)
databases.scope: The comprehensive commercial NP reference work — the traditional gold standard for coverage and curation
databases.compound_count: UNVERIFIABLE — paywalled. I confirmed the live product is 'Dictionary of Natural Products 35.1', CRC Press / Taylor & Francis, © 2026 (P2), but the site returns 'You are not within the network of a subscribing institution. Please sign in with an Individual User account to continue.' No compound count is exposed to unauthenticated users, so I will not quote one.
databases.licence: Proprietary commercial subscription. Not redistributable under any circumstances. Sold via ChemNetBase alongside the Combined Chemical Dictionary and Dictionary of Marine Natural Products.
databases.api_or_download_url: https://dnp.chemnetbase.com/ — resolves (HTTP 200) but gated behind institutional IP range or individual login. No API, no bulk download offered.
databases.suitability: EXCLUDE from an automated pipeline. Paywalled, no API, no bulk export, and licence terms forbid redistribution — so even with institutional access it cannot legally seed a shareable library. Its only defensible role is as a manual spot-check oracle for validating a handful of entries from the open sources. Version it as DNP 35.1 (2026) if you cite it.

databases.name: TCMSP (Traditional Chinese Medicine Systems Pharmacology)
databases.scope: TCM herbs, their chemical ingredients with predicted ADME, protein targets and disease links
databases.compound_count: TCMSP Version 2.3 (site header also lists CancerHSP 1.3, PreDC 1.0). Scraped from the browse endpoints on 2026-08-17: 13,729 ingredient records, 3,339 targets, 867 diseases, 502 herbs. These are embedded as JSON inside the browse.php pages, so the counts are exact for what the site serves.
databases.licence: No licence grant. Footer reads 'Copyright © 2012 - 2023 Lab of Systems Pharmacology. All Rights Reserved.' Redistribution is not permitted.
databases.api_or_download_url: https://tcmsp-e.com/ — browse data embedded in https://tcmsp-e.com/browse.php?qc=herbs|ingredients|targets|diseases. There is no download endpoint: /download.php, /login.php and /register.php all return 404, and the 'Download' markup on browse.php is HTML-commented out.
databases.suitability: Scrape-only and structure-poor — a weak pipeline dependency. The ingredient records carry only computed ADME descriptors (MOL_ID, molecule_name, mw, hdon, hacc, alogp, halflife, ob, caco2, bbb, dl, FASA, tpsa, rbn) with no SMILES or InChI in the browse feed, so you cannot build a structure library from it directly; structures would have to be resolved per-molecule or via another source. No API, no bulk file, all-rights-reserved copyright. If you need TCM ingredient-target links, prefer CMAUP (licensed ambiguity but real structures and a clean dump) and treat TCMSP as a cross-reference only — note SymMap already carries TCMSP IDs.

databases.name: SymMap
databases.scope: TCM herbs mapped to ingredients, targets, diseases and — distinctively — TCM and modern-medicine symptoms and syndromes
databases.compound_count: Version 2.0: 698 herbs, 26,035 ingredients, 20,965 targets, 14,086 diseases, 2,285 TCM symptoms, 1,148 MM symptoms, 233 syndromes (statistics table on the download page). I downloaded the ingredient file (SMIT) and counted 27,690 data rows, slightly above the stated 26,035 — the file appears to include suppressed/linked duplicate entries (there are explicit 'Suppress' and 'Link_ingredient_id' columns).
databases.licence: No licence grant. Download page states only 'Copyright © 2022, Beijing University of Chinese Medicine'. Not redistributable.
databases.api_or_download_url: http://www.symmap.org/download/ — XLSX files, e.g. http://www.symmap.org/static/download/V2.0/SymMap%20v2.0%2C%20SMIT%20file.xlsx. IMPORTANT: HTTPS is broken (https://www.symmap.org/ fails to connect, curl exit 000); only plain HTTP works. Any ingestion job that enforces TLS will fail against this host.
databases.suitability: Usable for symptom/syndrome mapping, useless as a structure source — and that is not obvious from the documentation. I parsed the SMIT ingredient workbook: the 'Molecule_structure' column is empty for all 27,690 rows, and only 11,632 rows (42%) carry a PubChem CID, so you can resolve structures for under half the ingredients even via cross-reference. Distribution is XLSX only (no CSV/TSV), which adds an openpyxl-class dependency. Combined with HTTP-only transport and an all-rights-reserved notice, treat SymMap as an annotation overlay keyed on its TCMID/TCM-ID/TCMSP cross-reference columns, not as a compound source.

databases.name: TCMID (Traditional Chinese Medicine Integrated Database)
databases.scope: TCM prescriptions, herbs, ingredients, targets and drugs (last major release TCMID 2.0)
databases.compound_count: UNVERIFIABLE — resource is dead. I will not quote published figures since I could not reach any instance to confirm them.
databases.api_or_download_url: http://www.megabionet.org/tcmid/ — DEAD. Traced the full chain: www.megabionet.org resolves via public DNS to 47.88.54.60, which returns HTTP 302 redirecting to http://47.100.169.139/tcmid, and that final host accepts no connection (curl exit 000). The bare domain megabionet.org is NXDOMAIN on both Google and Cloudflare DNS. So the service is not merely slow — the redirect target is gone.
databases.suitability: DO NOT PLAN AROUND THIS. Dead, with a redirect chain that dead-ends at an unreachable IP. Beware a naming collision that could produce a false positive in your own link-checking: https://bidd.group/TCMID/ returns HTTP 200, but that is TCM-ID (Traditional Chinese Medicine Information Database, BIDD/NUS) — a different resource, last updated October 2020, reporting 7,443 high-quality TCM prescriptions and 27,631 expression profiles, not compound structures. Do not substitute one for the other. TCMID content survives indirectly: SymMap and CMAUP both integrated it and expose TCMID cross-reference IDs.

databases.name: KNApSAcK
databases.scope: Species-metabolite relationships across plants and other organisms; the classic metabolite-organism pairing resource
databases.compound_count: 63,735 metabolites and 159,606 metabolite-species pairs, stated on the front page with 'last update 2026/07/03' — so the web database is actively curated. The downloadable release, however, is Version 1.200.03 dated 2008/12/19 (a 131 KB zip, which I downloaded and confirmed is a valid archive).
databases.licence: Explicitly restrictive. Verbatim from the Core System page: content 'cannot be re-distributed or used for commercial purposes by any user without contacting with KNApSAcK DB group'. This is the clearest prohibition in the survey — no redistribution, no commercial use.
databases.api_or_download_url: Web/pseudo-API documented at http://www.knapsackfamily.com/knapsack_core/top.php — http://www.knapsackfamily.com/knapsack_core/info.php?sname=[item]&word=[keyword] where item is one of organism, metabolite, formula, C_ID, CAS_ID (returns HTML, not JSON). Frozen bulk: http://www.knapsackfamily.com/KNApSAcK/dl/KNApSAcKforDL-v1.200.03.zip
databases.suitability: The 18-year gap between the live web data (updated 2026-07-03) and the only bulk download (2008-12-19) is the material finding — anyone who ingests the zip believing it reflects the stated 63,735 metabolites will be badly wrong. Getting current data means scraping info.php per query, which returns HTML you must parse, and doing so at scale against an academic host is both slow and impolite. Combined with an explicit no-redistribution, no-commercial-use clause, KNApSAcK is not a viable automated pipeline dependency. Use it for targeted manual lookups, or negotiate access with the NAIST group.

databases.name: UNPD (Universal Natural Products Database)
databases.scope: Broad universal NP collection assembled at Peking University; widely cited in 2010s NP cheminformatics
databases.compound_count: UNVERIFIABLE — resource is dead. No number quoted.
databases.api_or_download_url: http://pkuxxj.pku.edu.cn/UNPD/ — DEAD. The hostname still resolves in DNS (222.29.45.252) but no HTTP service answers on it; every request to the UNPD path, the index and the bare host times out with curl exit 000. This is the deceptive failure mode: DNS-only link checkers will report UNPD as alive.
databases.suitability: DO NOT PLAN AROUND THIS. Definitively unavailable. Its content is not entirely lost to the ecosystem — NPASS explicitly lists UNPD among the databases it mined for species-source annotation, and COCONUT aggregated UNPD historically — so ingesting COCONUT and NPASS recovers much of the chemistry. But UNPD itself cannot be fetched, and any dependency on it must be removed.

notes: VERIFICATION BASIS: every count, licence, URL and identifier above was retrieved live on 2026-08-17 via curl, the respective REST/SPARQL APIs, or by downloading and parsing the actual data files. Where I could not retrieve a number I wrote 'unverified' rather than estimating. Files I actually downloaded and counted: NPAtlas TSV (33.7 MB), NPASS structure file (61 MB), CMAUP ingredients/plants/activities, CyanoMetDB V03 CSV, LOTUS 260413_frozen.csv.gz, SymMap SMIT XLSX, a ZINC-22 NP SMILES shard, and the KNApSAcK 2008 zip.

THREE RESOURCES ARE DEAD AND MUST BE REMOVED FROM ANY PLAN. (1) SuperNatural III — bioinf-applied.charite.de is NXDOMAIN on both Google and Cloudflare DNS despite a 2023 NAR database-issue paper claiming ~449k unique NPs; no mirror exists and bio.tools still advertises the dead URL. (2) TCMID — megabionet.org/tcmid redirects through 47.88.54.60 to 47.100.169.139, which refuses connections. (3) UNPD — pkuxxj.pku.edu.cn still resolves in DNS but no HTTP service answers. These are exactly the 2010s-era NP databases the brief warned about.

TWO DISTINCT FAILURE MODES YOUR LINK-CHECKER MUST DISTINGUISH. NXDOMAIN (SuperNatural III) is honest failure — any checker catches it. DNS-resolves-but-no-service (UNPD) is the dangerous one: a naive availability check that only does a DNS lookup will mark UNPD healthy forever. Build the monitor around a real HTTP GET with a timeout and a content assertion, not a ping or a resolve.

NAMING COLLISION THAT WILL PRODUCE A FALSE POSITIVE: https://bidd.group/TCMID/ returns HTTP 200 and is linked from CMAUP, but it is TCM-ID (Traditional Chinese Medicine Information Database, BIDD/NUS, last updated Oct 2020, 7,443 prescriptions), NOT the dead TCMID (Traditional Chinese Medicine Integrated Database, megabionet). An automated resurrection check keyed on the string 'TCMID' will wrongly conclude the resource is alive.

REDISTRIBUTION TIERS — this is the axis that should drive your schema partitioning. Freely redistributable: LOTUS (Wikidata CC0 / Zenodo CC BY 4.0), CyanoMetDB (CC BY 4.0), COCONUT (CC0 per site, CC BY 4.0 per Zenodo — resolve before shipping), PubChem (no copyright restriction on the aggregation). Redistributable but copyleft: ChEMBL (CC BY-SA 3.0, verified from the FTP LICENSE file) — ShareAlike can infect a merged derivative, so keep it in its own partition. Non-commercial only: NPAtlas (CC BY-NC 4.0). Explicitly forbidden: KNApSAcK ('cannot be re-distributed or used for commercial purposes'). Licence-silent, therefore all-rights-reserved by default: NPASS, CMAUP, TCMSP, SymMap, ZINC-22. Proprietary: DNP.

THE LICENCE-SILENT GROUP IS THE BIGGEST LEGAL RISK, not the explicitly-restricted one. NPASS and CMAUP publish open bulk TSVs with no terms attached and are widely treated as open in the literature, but silence is not a grant. If this library will ever be shared or commercialised, get written permission from the BIDD group (Tsinghua/Fudan/NUS) for NPASS and CMAUP, or fence them off.

RECOMMENDED INGESTION CORE (all verified working, all machine-readable, ~1.2M molecules before dedup): COCONUT via the Zenodo dump for breadth, LOTUS frozen CSV for referenced organism provenance, NPAtlas TSV for microbial depth and perfect citation coverage, CyanoMetDB CSV for cyanobacteria, NPASS for measured bioactivity, CMAUP for plant-target-pathway links, and ChEMBL as a bioactivity join target. Join on InChIKey. LOTUS and Wikidata cross-validated to within 0.1% (227,319 vs 227,361 structures; 37,468 vs 37,550 organisms), which gives real confidence in that layer.

API TRAPS THAT COST ME TIME AND WILL SILENTLY CORRUPT A PIPELINE. COCONUT: the search parameter is 'query', not 'q' — passing 'q' is accepted and returns the entire 1,122,178-row table as if it were your result set, which is a perfect recipe for a fabricated count. COCONUT also caps deep pagination (pages 20000 and 40000 returned empty while 5000 worked), so the API cannot enumerate the full database. Wikidata: P703 'found in taxon' is used on genes and proteins as well as chemicals, so an unfiltered COUNT returns 2,574,092 subjects instead of ~227k chemicals — always constrain on P235 or P233. PubChem: classifications.fcgi ignores the hnid parameter and returns the whole tree regardless, hid=list returns HTTP 400, PUG-View annotations/heading 404s for all three NP headings, and Entrez [SRC] queries for NPASS/LOTUS/COCONUT all return 0.

TRANSPORT AND FORMAT GOTCHAS FOR A LAPTOP JOB. SymMap serves over plain HTTP only — HTTPS fails outright, so a TLS-enforcing client cannot reach it. SymMap and NPAtlas offer XLSX (SymMap XLSX-only), so you need an xlsx reader in the stack. COCONUT's open API requires POST, not GET. NPAtlas /api/v1 paths return HTTP 200 with empty bodies, which can look like a successful empty result rather than 'no API here'. ZINC-22's CartBlanche front end is a JavaScript SPA that yields nothing to curl.

STEREOCHEMISTRY COVERAGE, MEASURED NOT ASSUMED (fraction of structures with '@' in SMILES, or isomeric SMILES where noted): NPAtlas 73.7% tetrahedral and 27.8% E/Z; NPASS 73.2%; CyanoMetDB 73.9% tetrahedral with 75.8% having an isomeric SMILES; CMAUP 69.6%; LOTUS 76% carrying Wikidata isomeric SMILES (P2017); COCONUT 46.7% in a 300-molecule sample drawn from three widely separated API pages. The COCONUT figure is from the API's canonical_smiles field and a modest sample — verify against the Zenodo SDF, which carries dedicated stereo fields, before relying on it.

STALENESS GAPS BETWEEN LIVE DATA AND DOWNLOADABLE DATA — a reproducibility hazard. KNApSAcK is the extreme case: the web database was updated 2026-07-03 but the only bulk download is v1.200.03 from 2008-12-19, an 18-year gap. COCONUT is milder but real: the live API serves 1,122,178 molecules while the newest Zenodo dump is from 2024-10-04. Pin and record the exact artifact version you ingest; do not cite a live web count next to a dump you actually loaded.

SOURCE OVERLAP WILL INFLATE YOUR TOTALS IF UNMANAGED. NPASS integrates activity data from ChEMBL v35 and drew species-source annotation from TCM-ID, TCMID, TCM@Taiwan, COCONUT, TCMSP, UNPD, TM-MC, StreptomeDB, TTD, TarNet, ChEBI and HerDing. CyanoMetDB carries NPAtlas IDs for 85.1% of entries. SymMap integrates TCMID, TCMSP, TCM-ID, HIT, HERB and DCABM-TCM. PubChem re-exposes LOTUS (224,662), NPASS (82,207) and NPAtlas (37,365) as classification headings. Deduplicate on InChIKey and keep per-source attribution columns, or the merged count will be meaningless and licence provenance will be lost.

error_rates.figure: 22.1% of unique COCONUT molecules have MORE THAN ONE stereochemical version of their structure across sources (50% have exactly one). Sorokina & Steinbeck state verbatim these 'could be different valid stereoisomers of the same base constitution or errors in the databases.'

failure_modes.mode: Silent stereochemistry loss — records ingested with stereocentres present but unspecified
failure_modes.why_it_happens: Source databases inherit structures from aggregators that unified on stereochemistry-free InChIKeys, or from text-mined SMILES where wedge/hash information never survived. Sorokina & Steinbeck found 48,611 NPs (11.8% of COCONUT v1) with at least one stereocentre and no configuration; COCONUT 2.0 still carries 73,563 such records (12.0% of stereocentre-bearing entries) after full ChEMBL-pipeline curation.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Deterministic and cheap. RDKit: Chem.FindMolChiralCenters(mol, includeUnassigned=True, useLegacyImplementation=False) and Chem.FindPotentialStereo(mol); count entries where unspecified > 0. Also flag unspecified double-bond stereo (BondStereo.STEREOANY). Report implied_stereoisomers = 2^(unspecified centres) per record. The existing 8-compound set already does exactly this (data/validation_report.json flags '21 of 21 stereocentres are unspecified' for ginsenoside Rg1), so the check is already written — it just needs to become a gate, not a warning.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: At 12%, a 100,000-record corpus ships ~12,000 undockable ligands. Docking cannot choose among stereoisomers: ten Brink & Exner showed GOLD and PLANTS both fail to rank stereoisomers correctly. A ginsenoside with 21 unspecified centres has 2^21 ≈ 2.1 million implied stereoisomers — any single pose you generate is arbitrary, and every downstream affinity number derived from it is noise presented as a measurement. Worse than the 8-compound set, which at least records the defect.

failure_modes.mode: Stereochemical conflict — the same 2D constitution carries contradictory configurations from different sources
failure_modes.why_it_happens: 22.1% of unique COCONUT molecules have more than one stereochemical version. The aggregating authors themselves cannot say whether a given case is two genuine stereoisomers or one erroneous record. Cross-reference agreement between databases rises 15–20 percentage points (max +47.4) when stereochemistry is discarded — i.e. stereo disagreement is the single biggest reason two databases' 'same compound' records differ.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Group all incoming records by stereo-stripped InChIKey (first block of the standard InChIKey, or InChI generated with /SNon). Any group whose members have ≥2 distinct full InChIKeys with the same molecular formula is a conflict. Emit the conflict set for human adjudication; never silently pick one. Cross-check the resolved configuration against the isolation paper's reported [α]D or ECD where available.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: At 22%, more than one in five records in an ingested corpus is a coin-flip on configuration, and the pipeline has no principled tiebreaker. Automatic 'first source wins' or 'most common wins' resolution manufactures a confident-looking wrong answer at scale — and because the erroneous record is then re-exported, it propagates into every downstream aggregator (COCONUT 2.0 documents exactly this circular-import contamination).

failure_modes.mode: Published structure is simply wrong — misassigned constitution or configuration in the primary literature
failure_modes.why_it_happens: NP structures are assigned from spectroscopic evidence alone, usually without total synthesis or crystallography. Kutateladze's DU8+ computational NMR audit found a ~14% incidence of erroneous structures, matching Zimmerman's 1970s prediction of 10–22%. Shen, Appendino & Guo catalogued >200 misassigned marine NPs in 11 years alone. This error is upstream of every database and no amount of database curation removes it.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Not detectable by cheminformatics sanity checks — the structures are valence-legal and parse fine. Detectable only by (a) computational NMR re-prediction (DP4+, DU8+, CASE via ACD/Structure Elucidator) against the original reported shifts, which Elyashberg et al. showed recovers the correct structure in minutes for cases that took years by total synthesis; (b) checking whether the paper deposited raw FIDs (McAlpine et al.'s central recommendation); (c) checking whether the compound has ever been confirmed by X-ray or total synthesis. Encode this as a provenance tier per record, not a boolean.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: ~1 in 7 records is a molecule that does not exist. Every docking pose, every physicochemical descriptor, every ML training label attached to it is fiction. Critically, this is the one failure mode that scales *linearly with corpus size and cannot be filtered*, so it sets a hard ceiling on the quality of any automated expansion. Hand-curating 8 compounds against primary literature avoids this; ingesting 100,000 does not.

failure_modes.mode: Tautomer mismatch between deposited form and solution form; tautomeric duplicates
failure_modes.why_it_happens: Databases store whichever tautomer the depositor drew. Ring–chain tautomerism is possible for an average 16% of compounds in natural product and approved-drug databases; prototropic tautomerism for more than two-thirds of a 103M-record corpus. Curcumin is the exemplar: NMR shows it exists only as the enol tautomers, never the 1,3-diketone that is universally deposited and drawn. Separately, 1.09% of a 6M-entry commercial database consists of entries that are tautomeric duplicates of another entry in the same database (~30,000 such product pairs).
failure_modes.detectable_how: Enumerate tautomers with RDKit's rdMolStandardize.TautomerEnumerator and canonicalise; index the corpus on the canonical tautomer to find duplicate clusters. Separately flag records whose canonical tautomer differs from the deposited one — those are the docking risk. Note Guasch et al.'s warning that ring–chain transforms specifically can be over-aggressive and merge genuinely distinct compounds, so ring–chain merges must be surfaced for review rather than applied.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Docking the wrong tautomer changes H-bond donor/acceptor assignment at the pharmacophore, which is the dominant term in most scoring functions — the pose is not merely imprecise, it is mechanistically wrong. And 40% of tautomeric conflicts also involve a change in stereochemistry, so tautomer errors and stereo errors are correlated, not independent: a naive dedup pass can flip configuration while 'cleaning'.

failure_modes.mode: Duplicate inflation — corpus size reported in records, not compounds
failure_modes.why_it_happens: NP databases are largely copies of each other: 40 of 50 open NP databases overlap ≥50% with at least one other, and every one but the Lichen Database shares ≥10%. COCONUT 2.0's own pipeline shows the scale: ~1.5M imported entries collapse to 695,133 unique structures — 54% attrition. Ingesting N sources does not give N× the compounds.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Standard InChIKey exact match for hard duplicates; stereo-stripped InChIKey block for near-duplicates; canonical-tautomer key for tautomeric duplicates; Morgan/ECFP4 Tanimoto ≥0.99 for representation-only differences. Report unique-compound count and source-multiplicity histogram alongside any headline record count. Publish the deduplication cascade explicitly (imported → valence-valid → non-synthetic → unique) the way COCONUT 2.0 does.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: A corpus advertised as '400,000 natural products' may be ~185,000 distinct compounds. Duplicates also poison any train/test split: the same compound appearing in both halves under different source IDs produces inflated model performance that will not survive prospective testing. And weighting by record count silently upweights whichever compounds happen to be in the most databases (coumaric acid, gallic acid, scopoletin, ellagic acid are the top recurring entries) — the very promiscuous polyphenols most likely to be artifacts.

failure_modes.mode: Identifier–structure disagreement within a single record
failure_modes.why_it_happens: Records carry a MOL/connection table, a SMILES, an InChI, an IUPAC name and often a CAS number, generated at different times by different toolkits with different standardisation rules. Akhondi et al. measured internal MOL↔SMILES consistency as low as 37.2% (HMDB) and MOL↔IUPAC-name as low as 55.7%. Ingestion pipelines pick one field arbitrarily.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Regenerate every identifier from the connection table with a single pinned toolkit version and diff against the deposited value. RDKit: parse the MOL, emit canonical isomeric SMILES and standard InChI, compare to the record's stored strings. Log per-field disagreement rate per source; refuse to use a source's SMILES field if its regeneration agreement is below a stated threshold. Also compare the deposited molecular formula against the RDKit-computed one — the existing repo already does this ('rdkit_formula_matches').
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Whichever field the ingestion code happens to read determines which molecule you model, and the choice is silently different per source. Two pipelines built on the same 'database' will produce different corpora. This also makes provenance claims unfalsifiable: citing a PubChem CID guarantees nothing about the structure you actually used.

failure_modes.mode: Cross-reference chasing produces the wrong compound
failure_modes.why_it_happens: Pipelines resolve a name or an ID by following cross-references between databases. Agreement between cross-referenced MOL files ranges 25.8%–93.7%, typically 60–75%. The worst measured case is NPC→PubChem at 25.8% over 9,557 cross-references — partly because 1,527 NPC compounds carry more than one PubChem CID (mean 5.7, median 3). Single-cross-reference cases do better (79.3%) but still fail one time in five.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Never accept a cross-reference as an identity assertion. Verify structurally: pull the target record's connection table and compare standard InChIKeys. Flag one-to-many cross-references as unresolvable rather than picking the first. Record and report a per-source-pair agreement rate so the gate threshold is empirical, not assumed.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Silent compound substitution — you dock molecule B while your provenance trail says molecule A. This is the most corrosive failure mode because it is invisible in the output and destroys the audit trail. At 60–75% typical agreement, roughly a quarter to a third of any cross-reference-resolved corpus points somewhere other than where it claims.

failure_modes.mode: Bioactivity attributed to a compound when it was measured on a crude extract
failure_modes.why_it_happens: The largest NP bioactivity corpus, NAPRALERT, holds 400,000+ activity reports on extracts against 300,000+ on isolates — ~57% of reports are extract-level. Text-mining and record-linking pipelines routinely attach the extract's activity to the compound named in the same paper. By researchers' own survey responses, ~22% of medicinal-plant pharmacology studies characterise the extract half the time or less, and 7.7% never do.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Partly detectable: parse the assay-description field for extract vocabulary (extract, fraction, decoction, tincture, essential oil, % w/w, crude, methanolic/ethanolic/aqueous, bioassay-guided) and require an explicit purity statement or isolation reference before promoting a record to compound-level. Require a stated test-article concentration in molar units — extract data is almost always reported in µg/mL, which is a strong machine-readable signal. Records without a compound-level concentration should be tiered down, not dropped silently.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Activity attribution collapses. An IC50 measured on a whole extract cannot be assigned to the most abundant compound in it — that is the fallacy Nelson et al. call static residual complexity, and it is the leading explanation they offer for curcumin's apparent polypharmacology. At scale you build a structure–activity dataset in which a large fraction of the labels belong to unknown mixtures, then train a model that learns extract composition rather than molecular recognition.

failure_modes.mode: Colloidal aggregators ingested as genuine binders
failure_modes.why_it_happens: Aggregation is the dominant artifact mechanism in biochemical assays and aggregator-like compounds are ~7-fold enriched in the reported-bioactivity literature (5.1% of literature ligands active at 0.1–10 µM resemble a known aggregator, versus 0.73% of drug-like catalogue compounds), with that fraction up 9-fold since 1995. Most historical NP activity reports predate detergent counterscreens. In a fully mechanism-resolved screen, 95% of 1,274 apparent β-lactamase inhibitors were detergent-sensitive aggregators.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Highly detectable and cheap. Query Aggregator Advisor (advisor.bkslab.org) for Tanimoto ≥0.85 similarity to the >12,000 known aggregators, combined with cLogP and reported potency — the published prospective hit rates are 5/7 at Tc 0.95–0.99, 10/19 at 0.90–0.94, 3/7 at 0.85–0.89, so treat the flag as a graded prior, not a verdict. Or run ChemFH's DMPNN aggregator model (AUC 0.933–0.938) at ~2,500 molecules/min. Separately flag any activity record whose assay description lacks a detergent control (0.01% Triton X-100) or a DLS/enzyme-concentration-dependence counterscreen.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Aggregators are non-specific by definition, so they will dock plausibly against anything and will appear as multi-target hits, which an unwary pipeline reads as valuable polypharmacology. Because the literature is enriched 7-fold for them relative to catalogue space, an ingestion pipeline that samples from the *reported-active* literature — which is exactly what expanding from a hand-curated set means — preferentially harvests them.

failure_modes.mode: Frequent hitters / PAINS-class reactivity treated as target engagement
failure_modes.why_it_happens: NP chemical space is rich in catechols, quinones, Michael acceptors, β-diketones and polyphenols. Bisson et al.'s NAPRALERT mining identified 39 compounds dominating the reported-activity literature, over half of which are not explained by known synthetic-library artifact mechanisms. Curcumin exhibits every known PAINS behaviour simultaneously — covalent protein labelling, metal chelation, redox reactivity, aggregation, membrane disruption, fluorescence interference and structural decomposition.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Substructure alerts (RDKit FilterCatalog PAINS_A/B/C — 480 alerts) plus ChemFH's seven mechanism-specific models. CRITICALLY, do not use PAINS as an auto-reject: Capuzzi, Muratov & Tropsha showed 68% of the 480 alerts derive from four or fewer compounds, 97% of PubChem PAINS-containing compounds were infrequent hitters in the very assay technology the alerts came from, 109 alerts occur in Dark Chemical Matter, and 87 FDA-approved drugs contain them. Use alerts to set a review tier and to require orthogonal evidence, not to delete.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Two symmetric failures. Auto-rejecting on PAINS at 100,000-record scale discards a large slice of legitimate NP chemistry (approved drugs included) with a ~97% false-positive rate. Auto-accepting ingests the frequent hitters that already dominate NP activity reports. Neither is acceptable, which means this failure mode forces a human-review tier that does not scale — the central argument against unbounded automated expansion.

failure_modes.why_it_happens: Polyphenols, quinones and catechols — heavily represented in NP corpora — generate micromolar H2O2 in the DTT/TCEP-containing buffers standard in HTS. The H2O2 then oxidises accessible Cys/Trp/Met/His/Sec residues, inactivating protein tyrosine phosphatases, cysteine proteases and metalloenzymes. The apparent inhibition is real and reproducible but has nothing to do with binding.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Substructure alerts for catechol, hydroquinone, para/ortho-quinone and related redox-active motifs; ChemFH includes a reactive-compound model. At the record level, flag any activity whose target is a Cys-dependent enzyme AND whose assay buffer contained a strong reducing agent AND whose compound carries a redox alert — that triple is a strong machine-detectable prior. A published prevalence rate for NP libraries specifically is UNVERIFIED; if you need it, measure it locally on your own corpus and state the RDKit version and SMARTS set used.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Systematically corrupts entire target classes rather than random records. Every phosphatase, cathepsin and metalloprotease activity record sourced from reducing-buffer assays becomes suspect at once, so the corruption is correlated by target — which means it will not average out and will instead teach any downstream model a false structure–activity rule ('polyphenols inhibit phosphatases').

failure_modes.mode: Assay-readout interference from intrinsic fluorescence or absorbance
failure_modes.why_it_happens: Many NP chromophores absorb and emit inside the windows used by fluorescence, FRET, AlphaScreen and luciferase assays. Curcumin absorbs at ~408–500 nm and emits at ~450–600 nm — squarely inside common bioassay readout bands. In the NIH MLPCN tau-fibril campaign it scored IC50 3.5 µM in a thioflavin-T fluorescence qHTS, was inactive in a fluorescence-polarisation secondary assay, and was active in a total-fluorescence counterscreen at IC50 13 µM.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Two independent checks. (a) Structure-side: ChemFH's fluorescent-compound and firefly-luciferase-inhibitor models; extended-conjugation and fused-aromatic descriptors. (b) Record-side, and more decisive: flag any activity record whose only supporting assay is a single fluorescence/luminescence readout with no orthogonal or label-free confirmation (SPR, ITC, X-ray, CETSA). Nelson et al. note NAPRALERT's dominant reported activities come from cellular assays that use fluorescence/quenching endpoints, so this filter bites hard on NP data specifically.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Because interference tracks the chromophore, it is again correlated rather than random: whole compound classes (curcuminoids, flavonoids, anthraquinones, coumarins) acquire spurious activity against unrelated targets. This is a large part of the mechanism by which curcumin accumulated 28 pharmacological activities representing ~50% of its reported effects — a ratio 25× higher than for artemisinin, ivermectin or paclitaxel.

failure_modes.mode: Activity values ingested as independent measurements when they are re-citations of one experiment
failure_modes.why_it_happens: 90% of matched Ki pairs in ChEMBL are repeated citations of a single measurement rather than independent replicates. Reviews, follow-up papers and secondary databases re-report the same number, and aggregation pipelines count each occurrence.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Deduplicate activity records on (compound InChIKey, target, assay type, value) before doing anything statistical; trace document IDs back to the earliest reporting paper and keep a citation graph. Treat identical values to two decimal places on the same compound-target pair as one measurement unless the assay descriptions differ materially. Also screen for unit-transcription errors (nM/µM confusion produces characteristic 1,000-fold outliers within a compound-target group) and for undifferentiated stereoisomers collapsed onto one activity.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Fabricated confidence. A value cited eleven times looks like eleven independent confirmations and will be weighted as such, producing artificially tight error bars around a number that may be a transcription error. Kramer et al.'s corrected uncertainty — mean error 0.44 pKi, SD 0.54 — caps the maximum achievable R² for any model at ~0.81; a pipeline that treats re-citations as replicates will report cross-validated R² above that ceiling and be, by construction, overtrained.

failure_modes.mode: Synthetic and non-natural compounds contaminating a 'natural products' corpus
failure_modes.why_it_happens: Source databases mislabel drug derivatives and synthetics as NPs, and because organisms in the Anthropocene are exposed to synthetic chemicals, genuine synthetics get isolated from natural matrices. COCONUT 2.0 removes fluorinated compounds, sulfonamides and drug derivatives explicitly and still states that 'invalid entries will remain'; the NP-likeness score distribution retains substantial density below zero, indicating persistent synthetic content after curation.
failure_modes.detectable_how: NP-likeness score (RDKit's npscorer with the published model) — flag records below zero for review. Element-based alerts (F, and to a lesser degree Cl/Br patterns typical of synthesis), sulfonamide and other rare-in-nature functional groups, with an explicit exception list since genuine fluorinated and sulfonamide NPs exist. Require a source organism plus an isolation reference; records with neither are not natural-product records regardless of which database they came from.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Undermines the scientific rationale for the corpus. If the argument for NP expansion is privileged natural chemical space, a corpus silently diluted with synthetics does not deliver it. It also breaks organism-linked and biosynthesis-linked reasoning, and it means any 'natural product' claim made from the corpus is unsafe to publish.

failure_modes.why_it_happens: Text-mined and hand-typed SMILES fail to kekulise, exceed valence limits, or carry malformed aromatic ring perception. COCONUT 2.0 runs every entry through the ChEMBL Structure Curation Pipeline Checker and discards anything with error code six or higher — and notes that such valence errors propagate across datasets and versions through circular imports. This is not hypothetical here: the repo's own data/validation_report.json shows Huperzine A's platform SMILES failing RDKit kekulisation, one of four broken entries in a hand-curated set of eight.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Fully deterministic. Chem.MolFromSmiles/MolFromMolBlock with sanitize=True; run the ChEMBL structure_pipeline Checker and record the error code per entry. Compare RDKit-computed molecular formula and exact mass against the deposited values. Never write a record whose structure did not round-trip through parse → canonicalise → reparse.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: The cheapest and least interesting failure mode, and the only one automation genuinely fixes better than a human. But note the base rate: a hand-curated set of 8 had 4 broken SMILES (50%). That is the honest baseline the expansion is being compared against — automation will beat 50% here easily, which is precisely why this failure mode should not be used to justify the expansion. The hard modes above are the ones that decide it.

failure_modes.why_it_happens: Of 123 NP resources published since 2000, only 50 still had retrievable structures at the time of the 2020 review; several published shortly before the review were already inaccessible. Only 40% offer bulk download. Rich metadata (targets, toxicity, therapeutic effect) from defunct databases survives only as bare structures in ZINC, with the annotations lost.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Store, per record, the source database name, version/release date, retrieval date, retrieval URL and a content hash of the downloaded file. Re-resolve a random sample of source URLs on a schedule and report the decay rate. Refuse to ingest from a source that cannot supply a versioned bulk download — a scraped web interface is not a citable provenance chain.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: Non-reproducibility of the corpus itself. If a reviewer cannot re-derive the dataset from its stated sources, the corpus is not evidence, and no downstream result built on it can be defended. This is the one respect in which the 8-compound hand-curated set is unambiguously superior: each entry's provenance is short enough to re-verify by hand, and the repo already records per-field provenance and preserves retracted claims separately.

failure_modes.mode: Aggregate consequence — no verified reproducibility rate exists for natural-product activity claims specifically
failure_modes.why_it_happens: No NP-specific replication study was found this session. The closest defensible anchor is preclinical cancer biology, where the Reproducibility Project completed only 50 of 193 selected experiments (74% blocked by missing protocols, data or reagents), replicated 40% of positive effects, and found median replication effect sizes 85% smaller than original with 92% of replications smaller and only 3% larger.
failure_modes.detectable_how: Not detectable per record. Manage it as an explicit, quantified prior attached to every activity claim in the corpus: tag each record with the evidence tier that actually supports it (orthogonal-assay-confirmed / single-assay / extract-level / review-citation-only) and refuse to let untiered records drive any conclusion. This is a design requirement on the schema, not a filter.
failure_modes.consequence_at_scale: The compounding arithmetic is the whole decision. Independent-ish per-record failure probabilities: ~14% wrong structure, ~12% undefined stereo, ~22% conflicting stereo, ~57% of activity reports extract-level, ~5% aggregator-like among reported micromolar actives, and a preclinical replication rate around 40–46% for the underlying biology. Even generously, the joint probability that a randomly ingested NP record has a correct structure with defined and non-conflicting stereochemistry, an activity measured on the pure compound, no dominant interference mechanism, and a replicable underlying result is in the low single-digit percent. Expanding 8 hand-verified entries to a database-scale corpus therefore buys volume at a per-record correctness that is roughly an order of magnitude worse — unless the pipeline ships the tiering and gating above and reports the surviving high-confidence subset as the deliverable rather than the raw record count.

papers.title: Consistency of systematic chemical identifiers within and between small-molecule databases
papers.id: PMID 23237381 / PMC3539895 / DOI 10.1186/1758-2946-4-35 (Akhondi et al., J Cheminform 4:35)
papers.finding: Internal MOL-to-identifier consistency 37.2%-98.5% (MOL-SMILES: HMDB 37.2%, NPC 93.4%, ChEBI 96.5%, PubChem 97.8%, DrugBank 98.5%; MOL-IUPAC: HMDB 55.7%, ChEBI 75.3%, PubChem 87.2%, DrugBank 90.0%). Cross-database MOL agreement via cross-references 25.8%-93.7%, typically 60-75%; NPC-to-PubChem 25.8% over 9,557 links. Discarding stereochemistry raises agreement to 47.6%-95.6% (+15-20 points typical, +47.4 max), proving stereochemistry is the dominant cause of cross-database structural disagreement. Also the source of the widely quoted Williams & Ekins '>70% errors in absolute structural integrity, vs the 5-10% anticipated'. Full text read this session.

papers.title: COCONUT 2.0: a comprehensive overhaul and curation of the collection of open natural products database
papers.id: PMID 39588778 / PMC11701633 / DOI 10.1093/nar/gkae1063 (Chandrasekhar et al., Nucleic Acids Res)
papers.finding: ~1.5M imported entries from 63 sources collapse to 1,022,536 after ChEMBL Checker valence filtering and synthetic/multi-component removal, then to 695,133 unique NPs (Sept 2024) — 54% total attrition. Composition: 82,220 with no stereocentres, 539,350 with preserved stereochemistry, 73,563 with stereocentres but absolute configuration undefined (12.0% of stereocentre-bearing records, post-curation). Authors state circular imports between NP databases propagate valence errors and misclassified synthetics across datasets and versions, and that 'invalid entries will remain'. NP-likeness distribution shows persistent synthetic contamination. Full text read this session.

papers.title: Review on natural products databases: where to find data in 2020
papers.id: PMID 33431011 / PMC7118820 / DOI 10.1186/s13321-020-00424-9 (Sorokina & Steinbeck, J Cheminform 12:20)
papers.finding: 123 NP resources published/cited since 2000; 92 still accessible; only 50 with retrievable structures. COCONUT v1 = 411,621 unique molecules unified on stereochemistry-free InChIKeys. 27.9% have no stereocentres defined in any source; of those 57.7% (66,374) genuinely have none and 48,611 (11.8% of the whole database) have stereocentres with the information absent. 22.1% of unique molecules carry MORE THAN ONE stereochemical version — 'valid stereoisomers or errors in the databases'. 40 of 50 databases overlap >=50% with another; only 40% offer bulk download. Full text read this session.

papers.title: Experimental and Chemoinformatics Study of Tautomerism in a Database of Commercially Available Screening Samples
papers.id: PMID 27669079 / PMC5129033 / DOI 10.1021/acs.jcim.6b00338 (Guasch, Yapamudiyansel, Peach, Kelley, Barchi & Nicklaus, J Chem Inf Model 56:2149-2161)
papers.finding: ~30,000 cases in the 6M-entry Aldrich Market Select database where two or more products are the same compound in different tautomeric forms; 62,869 molecules (1.09%) are tautomeric duplicates of another same-database entry. 40% of tautomeric conflicts involve a change in stereochemistry. 81.2% require one transform step, 17.4% two. Prototropic tautomerism is possible for >2/3 of unique structures in a 103M-record corpus; ring-chain tautomerism for >8% of AMS and an average 16% of compounds in NATURAL PRODUCT and approved-drug databases. 166 tautomer pairs/triplets purchased and checked by 1H/13C NMR; ring-chain transforms found to be over-aggressive. Full text read this session.

papers.title: The value of universally available raw NMR data for transparency, reproducibility, and integrity in natural product research
papers.id: PMID 30003207 / PMC6350634 / DOI 10.1039/c7np00064b (McAlpine et al., Nat Prod Rep 36:35-107)
papers.finding: Reports a ca. 14% incidence rate of erroneous natural-product structures found by Kutateladze and co-workers via DU8+ computational NMR, matching Zimmerman's predicted 10-22% probability of misassignment from spectroscopic evidence alone. Documents concrete cases where absent raw FIDs made revision impossible, where impurity signals were mistaken for compound signals, and where transcribed chemical-shift tables contained typos. Full text read this session.

papers.title: Pitfalls in the structural elucidation of small molecules. A critical analysis of a decade of structural misassignments of marine natural products
papers.id: PMID 35770685 / DOI 10.1039/d2np00023g (Shen, Appendino & Guo, Nat Prod Rep 39:1803-1832)
papers.finding: >200 cases of misassigned MARINE natural products reported July 2010 - August 2021 (~18/yr, marine subset only), sorted by structural element. Notes distinct misassignment 'trends' between marine and plant-derived compounds, with a lower incidence of outright impossible structures among marine misassignments. Abstract retrieved this session.

papers.title: Enhancing Efficiency of Natural Product Structure Revision: Leveraging CASE and DFT over Total Synthesis
papers.id: PMID 37175206 / PMC10180399 / DOI 10.3390/molecules28093796 (Elyashberg, Tyagarajan et al., Molecules 28:3796)
papers.finding: Twelve real NP structure revisions that had required total synthesis were re-solved by Computer-Assisted Structure Elucidation plus DFT from the ORIGINALLY PUBLISHED NMR/MS data, in minutes to hours, in every case — including cases where the original data were incomplete or contained misassigned shifts. Establishes that computational structure verification is a tractable ingestion-time gate rather than a research project. Full text read this session.

papers.title: The Essential Medicinal Chemistry of Curcumin
papers.id: PMID 28074653 / PMC5346970 / DOI 10.1021/acs.jmedchem.6b00975 (Nelson, Dahlin, Bisson, Graham, Pauli & Walters, J Med Chem 60:1620-1637)
papers.finding: >15,000 manuscripts on curcumin biology (~50/week); >120 clinical trials; no successful double-blinded placebo-controlled trial and never conclusively effective in any randomized placebo-controlled trial; >$150M US federal funding since 1995 per NIH RePORTER. T-half <5 min, F <1%, solubility 1-10 ug/mL. Exhibits every known PAINS behaviour (covalent labelling, metal chelation, redox reactivity, aggregation, membrane disruption, fluorescence interference at 408-500/450-600 nm, decomposition). Exists in solution only as enol tautomers, not the deposited diketone. NAPRALERT statistics: 190,000+ references, 200,000+ compounds, 60,000+ organisms, 400,000+ EXTRACT bioactivity reports vs 300,000+ ISOLATE reports (~57% extract-level). 28 activities (<10% of categories) = ~50% of curcumin's reported activities vs 1-2% for artemisinin/ivermectin/paclitaxel. Full text read this session.

papers.title: Can Invalid Bioactives Undermine Natural Product-Based Drug Discovery?
papers.id: PMID 26505758 / PMC4791574 / DOI 10.1021/acs.jmedchem.5b01009 (Bisson, McAlpine, Friesen, Chen, Graham & Pauli, J Med Chem 59:1671-1690)

papers.title: The experimental uncertainty of heterogeneous public Ki data
papers.id: PMID 22643060 / DOI 10.1021/jm300131x (Kramer, Kalliokoski, Gedeck & Vulpetti, J Med Chem 55:5165-5173)
papers.finding: ChEMBL contains unit-transcription errors, undifferentiated stereoisomers, and repeated citations of single measurements accounting for 90% of all matched pairs. After filtering, true experimental uncertainty is mean error 0.44 pKi, SD 0.54, median 0.34; maximum achievable R-squared on large datasets is ~0.81. Any model reporting better than that ceiling is overtrained on duplicated data. Abstract retrieved this session.

papers.id: PMID 23613770 / PMC3628986 / DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0061007 (Kalliokoski, Kramer, Vulpetti & Gedeck, PLoS One 8:e61007)
